introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 2 (0525), ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: You are required to answer ANY FIVE questions. ONLY THE FIRST FIVE QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Les sous-parties (i), (ii), (iii)... restent dans le texte de la sous-question (a), (b) ou (c), dont `points` est la somme imprimée.

Question 1(a) : les quatre énoncés sont des définitions d'économies d'échelle internes, rattachées aux types usuels du programme (financières, de marketing, de risque, techniques) ; l'énoncé (ii) pourrait être rattaché par certains manuels aux « commercial economies », synonyme de marketing economies, indiqué dans le corrigé. Le sujet imprime « experts' sales men » et « by an increase in the demand for other » : recopiés tels quels.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the following internal economies of scale;

(i) Large firms find it easier to borrow from financial houses because they have valuable assets for use as collateral.

(ii) The ability for large firms to hire experts' sales men and expert buyers to reduce sales cost or huge discounts respectively.

(iii) When large firms produce varieties such that a fall in the price of one can be made good by an increase in the demand for other.

(iv) The ability of large firms to make better use of large equipment, specialization, full use of machines and better use of capital assets without use of smaller models.

1+1+1+1 (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Internal economies of scale are the **fall in a firm's average (unit) cost of production that results from the growth of the firm itself** (not of the whole industry). They are usually grouped as financial, marketing, risk-bearing, technical and managerial economies. Each statement describes one of these types.

| | Statement | Type of internal economy | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) | Large firms borrow more easily because they own valuable assets that can be used as collateral. | **Financial economies** | A large firm is seen as safe by banks, so it obtains loans more easily and often at a lower rate of interest, which lowers its financing cost per unit. |
| (ii) | Large firms hire expert salesmen and expert buyers; they reduce selling cost and obtain huge discounts. | **Marketing (commercial) economies** | Buying in bulk gives trade discounts, and specialist sales staff, large advertising campaigns and bulk transport spread the selling cost over many units. |
| (iii) | A large firm produces varieties, so a fall in the price of one can be made good by a rise in the demand for another. | **Risk-bearing economies** (diversification) | By spreading its output over several products and markets, the firm is protected against a fall in the demand for, or the price of, one product. |
| (iv) | A large firm makes better use of large equipment and specialisation, and fully uses its machines. | **Technical economies** (economies of large machines, indivisibilities) | Large and efficient machines can be bought and kept fully busy, and work is divided into specialised tasks, so the cost per unit falls. |

**Answers: (i) financial economies; (ii) marketing economies; (iii) risk-bearing economies (diversification); (iv) technical economies.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
State and explain Four (4) external economies of scale.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** External economies of scale are the **advantages that lower the average cost of all the firms in an industry as the whole industry grows**, whatever the size of the individual firm. They come from outside the firm, often from the concentration of firms in one area (for example, a cluster of timber firms or of cocoa processors).

1. **Concentration (localisation) of skilled labour.** When many firms of the same industry settle in one area, a pool of trained workers develops. Firms can recruit skilled workers easily and spend less on training, so their cost per unit falls.

2. **Growth of ancillary (supporting) firms.** Specialist suppliers of raw materials, spare parts, packaging and repair services settle near the industry. Firms buy inputs more cheaply and quickly, and transport costs are reduced.

3. **Development of infrastructure and public services.** A large industry attracts good roads, electricity, water, banks and insurance services to the area. All the firms share these facilities, so no single firm has to pay for them alone.

4. **Co-operation, research and shared information.** Firms in a big industry set up trade associations, training centres and research bodies and share information on markets and techniques. The cost of research and marketing is shared among many firms, which lowers each firm's cost.

(Other correct points: by-product industries that use the waste of the industry, and a good reputation of the area for the product, which makes selling easier.)

**Conclusion.** External economies of scale reduce the costs of every firm in the industry, so the industry can expand and sell at lower prices.

questions.enonce_markdown:
State and explain Four (4) reasons why firms grow in size.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A firm grows in size when it increases its output, capital, labour force and market. Growth may be **internal** (ploughing back profits, opening new branches) or **external** (merger, takeover). Firms grow for the following reasons.

1. **To enjoy economies of scale.** A larger firm can buy in bulk, use large machines and spread its fixed costs, so its average cost falls and its profit per unit rises.

2. **To increase market share and market power.** By growing, or by joining with a competitor, a firm sells more and faces less competition. It may then have more influence over the price it charges and over its suppliers.

3. **To spread risk (diversification).** A firm that produces several products or sells in several markets is protected if the demand for one product falls. Growth into new products or regions therefore makes the firm more secure.

4. **To increase profit and satisfy the ambition of owners and managers.** Bigger sales usually bring higher total profit, and owners and managers may want more power, higher salaries and prestige. Profits kept in the business are used to expand.

(Other correct points: to secure the supply of raw materials or outlets for its products, by vertical integration; to avoid being taken over by a larger rival; and to obtain more finance, because a large firm can raise capital more easily.)

**Conclusion.** The main aim of growth is to reduce cost, earn more profit and survive in competition.
